findings.title: Collision recovery deletes the value it should keep
findings.description: The collision rule tells the user to clear a stale shared-file copy with `cf config unset git.integration_branch --project`. Verification step 9 (line 259) repeats this and expects `cf check` to come back clean. But line 89 says delete "deletes from whichever project file the key's scope maps to," and this key is `personal`. So `unset --project` removes `legacy/value` from `.context-forge.local.toml` and leaves the stale shared copy in place. The read fallback then resolves to `another-legacy-value`, and the `cf check` warning persists because the shared copy still exists. The recovery path does the opposite of what the text says. Add a file-targeted way to clear the shared copy and rewrite step 9 to match.

findings.title: No file-level config access for `migrate-personal` or the checker
findings.description: The design keeps the `ConfigManager` API unchanged (lines 49, 181) and says the existing TOML helpers are "reused as-is" against whichever path is selected (line 93). Neither holds. The helpers are module-private, and the public methods take a key and a user/project scope, not a file. Two new consumers need file-level access. `migrate-personal` must read personal-scope keys from the shared file and delete them there (line 144). The `ConsistencyChecker` rule must read the shared file's raw keys (line 142). Routing by key scope cannot express either. Exporting the helpers adds public surface the design says it doesn't add. Having CLI or introspection code parse TOML directly breaks the layering. This is the same gap behind the FAIL above. Declare the accessor in the API Contracts section before implementation.

findings.title: The gitignore line is written only by `cf init`, so the leak stays open
findings.description: The slice's stated value (line 23) is keeping personal settings out of commits. The plan calls the current gitignore decision "left entirely to the user." But the ignore line is written only from `cf init` (line 158), and the success criterion (line 216) covers only fresh projects. Any project that predates this slice, or where a user runs `cf config set git.integration_branch ... --project` or `migrate-personal` without re-running `cf init`, gets `.context-forge.local.toml` with no ignore entry. The next `git add -A` commits it. Line 32 also says the line reuses "the pattern already used for personal ignores," but line 158 says no gitignore logic exists, so there is nothing to reuse. Decide where the ignore guarantee lives: on the personal-file write path, or as a `cf check` finding when the personal file exists and is not ignored. Otherwise record the exposure as an accepted risk.

findings.title: Teammates silently lose the shared value after migration
findings.description: The migration story covers only the developer who runs `migrate-personal`. Once that developer commits the shared file without the key, every teammate who has no personal copy resolves `git.integration_branch` to unset or default on pull. Nothing fires for them. The read fallback (line 140) helps only while the key is still in the shared file, and the detection rule (line 142) fires only for personal keys still there. This contradicts the design's own goal at line 138: "Reads must not silently drop that value out from under the user." State the expected teammate step (each developer runs `cf config set ... --project` once) and surface it in the migrate output, or accept the silent change in the Risk Assessment.

findings.title: Failure modes are not observable to scripts and have no tests
findings.description:
The write-personal-then-delete-shared ordering (line 149) is correct. Three gaps remain:
- `migrate-personal` reports per-key `failed: <error>` in its summary, but the design never says the exit code becomes non-zero. A CI or script sees success after a partial failure.
- The new `ConsistencyChecker` read of the shared file (line 142) has no stated handling for unreadable or malformed TOML. The design doesn't say whether it throws or emits a finding.
- The test list (line 222) covers only the happy path and no-op path. The collision branch (line 146), the per-key failure path, and the checker read failure have no tests. Each failure mode needs an observable signal and at least one test that asserts it.

findings.title: Scope is heavier than the plan requires
findings.description:
The plan asks for classification, routing, the gitignore line, a migration story, and the MCP surface. The design adds weight that can be cut:
- The Verification Walkthrough (lines 225–259) restates the Functional Requirements (lines 212–218) nearly item for item. Keep one. Development Approach (lines 273–281) also repeats Component Structure (lines 55–73).
- The `'project-personal'` source tier (lines 181–188) is not in the plan and is used only for display. Verification steps 4 and 8 can check the files directly. Defer it unless the Project Manager asks.
- Per-key failure continuation in `migrate-personal` (line 149) adds a code path. The command is idempotent and the read fallback keeps values resolving, so abort-on-first-failure is equally recoverable.
- The identical-value deletion branch (line 146) is optional. Skipping and reporting any key already in the personal file leaves one collision rule. Identical values then stay flagged until the explicit unset.

findings.title: Scope literals and the personal filename are repeated
findings.description: Routing compares against the `'personal'` and `'shared'` literals (lines 78, 84–86). The checker repeats `=== 'personal'` (line 142). The filename `.context-forge.local.toml` appears as a literal in the gitignore step (line 158), the path helper (line 177), and the CLI output (line 197). Project rules require each comparison value to be defined once. Specify one scope constant and one filename constant, owned by `configPaths`, and have init, the checker, and the CLI reference them.

findings.title: A prerequisite the design relies on is not in the plan
findings.description: The frontmatter lists only `dependencies: [914]` (line 6). The plan entry says `Dependencies: none`. The body says the scope-resolution bug was "fixed ad hoc as a 916 prerequisite" and is "already merged to main" (line 46). But the plan's 916 is "Guide Update Branch Guard," and no plan entry records a config-scope fix. Either record the change in the plan under its real identifier or drop the claim. Also align the frontmatter with the plan on 914 (already done, so not blocking).

findings.title: Naming and table details
findings.description: Precedence is named `project-shared` (line 124), but the `ConfigResult.source` union uses `'project'` for the same file (line 186). Pick one. The classification table (line 109) lists `workflow.review_gates.*.threshold` as one row, but the registry has four explicit entries (code, arch, slice, tasks), and each needs its own `scope` field. List them explicitly.

findings.title: Plan scope is fully covered
findings.description: Each item in the 915 plan entry maps to a design section: registry classification, file routing, precedence, the `cf init` gitignore line, the migration and compatibility story, and the MCP config surface. The explicit exclusions (lines 36–40) keep the `cf config set` surface unchanged. The design defers nothing the plan assigns to this slice. The precedence change extends the existing user-vs-project merge rather than adding a new mechanism, as the plan asks.

findings.title: Routing stays inside `ConfigManager`
findings.description: Callers keep passing `scope: 'project'`, and the design explicitly rejects a third scope value. That keeps the dependency direction (callers → `ConfigManager` → registry) and matches the plan's "route through ConfigManager/configPaths.ts." The gap in the contract finding above is limited to the two new file-level consumers. Existing callers are unaffected.
